title: Chapter XXIX

teacherSummary.text: At Rosings, Lady Catherine dominates the conversation, questions Elizabeth about her family and education, and is surprised when Elizabeth answers boldly and will not state her age.

vocabulary.definition: A game at cards, played by two or more persons, usually for twenty-one points
vocabulary.context: Collins sat down to quadrille; and as Miss de Bourgh chose to play at cassino, the two girls had the honour of assisting Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cassino”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: The act or art of setting glass
vocabulary.context: Collins expected the scene to inspire, and was but slightly affected by his enumeration of the windows in front of the house, and his relation of what the glazing altogether had originally cost Sir Lewis de Bourgh.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “glazing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Her air was not conciliating, nor was her manner of receiving them, such as to make her visitors forget their inferior rank.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “conciliate”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To tell or utter so that another may write down
vocabulary.context: Elizabeth found that nothing was beneath this great Lady’s attention, which could furnish her with an occasion of dictating to others.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “dictate”: dict (Latin dicere, "to say") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To excel or exceed in power
vocabulary.context: Collins was carefully instructing them in what they were to expect, that the sight of such rooms, so many servants, and so splendid a dinner might not wholly overpower them.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overpower”: over- (Old English ofer, "over") + -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: “Aye, no doubt; but that is what a governess will prevent, and if I had known your mother, I should have advised her most strenuously to engage one.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “strenuous”: -ous (Latin -osus, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Jenkinson was chiefly employed in watching how little Miss de Bourgh ate, pressing her to try some other dish, and fearing she were indisposed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “indispose”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: An involuntary trembling, sometimes an effect of paralysis, but usually caused by terror or fear
vocabulary.context: She had heard nothing of Lady Catherine that spoke her awful from any extraordinary talents or miraculous virtue, and the mere stateliness of money and rank, she thought she could witness without trepidation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “trepidation”: -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Elizabeth found herself quite equal to the scene, and could observe the three ladies before her composedly.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “composed”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + pos (Latin ponere, "to place") + -ed (Old English -ed, past or "having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A chamber or apartment before the chief apartment and leading into it, in which persons wait for audience
vocabulary.context: Collins pointed out, with a rapturous air, the fine proportion and finished ornaments, they followed the servants through an antechamber, to the room where Lady Catherine, her daughter, and Mrs.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “antechamber”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Aristocrats expected deference; governesses and accomplishments signaled status.

significance: Elizabeth's independence before rank sets up her later confrontation with Lady Catherine.
discussionQuestions: What does Elizabeth's refusal to state her age show?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with class and social mobility?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXIX,” how does Austen show an imperious hostess? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXIX, how does Austen develop the idea of an imperious hostess? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXIX develops the idea of an imperious hostess. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXIX (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of an imperious hostess. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXIX suggests about an imperious hostess. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXIX to complicate the reader's understanding of an imperious hostess. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXIX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of an imperious hostess responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXIX alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of an imperious hostess follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXIX and its treatment of an imperious hostess. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXIX as evidence for a larger claim about an imperious hostess in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXIX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of an imperious hostess. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: Scarcely anything was talked of the whole day or next morning, but their visit to Rosings. Mr. Collins was carefully instructing them in what they were to expect, that the sight of such rooms, so many servants, and so splendid a dinner might not wholly overpower them.

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Setting
annotationFocus.lookFor: where and when events happen and how place shapes action or feeling

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does Elizabeth's refusal to state her age show? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are cassino, glazing, conciliating, dictating, overpower. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Collins sat down to quadrille; and as Miss de Bourgh chose to play at cassino, the two girls had the honour of assisting Mrs.” Webster's says: A game at cards, played by two or more persons, usually for twenty-one points. Now the word history: “cassino”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “glazing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it. “conciliate”: con- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Aristocrats expected deference; governesses and accomplishments signaled status. Why does this chapter matter? Elizabeth's independence before rank sets up her later confrontation with Lady Catherine. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to an imperious hostess.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Setting.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Scarcely anything was talked of the whole day or next morning, but their visit to Rosings. Mr. Collins was carefully instructing them in what they were to expect, that the sight of such rooms, so many servants, and so splendid a dinner might not wholly overpower them.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Irony, Setting: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXIX,” how does Austen show an imperious hostess? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about an imperious hostess, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes an imperious hostess. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
